title: Time Series: Moving Averages & Seasonal Component
sub: Lecture 6 · Seminar 7 · moving averages, seasonal differences & indices, regression approach
blurb: Smoothing a time series with simple and centred moving averages, choosing m, seasonal differences and indices by the simple approach, and the regression approach with dummy variables.
h1: Time Series: Moving Averages & the Seasonal Component
lede: Moving averages smooth a time series and give its trend. With the trend in hand, you can measure how strongly each season pushes the values up or down: by seasonal differences (additive) or seasonal indices (multiplicative), either in separate steps or with one regression.
six: A **moving average** smooths a series; the smoothed values are the **trend component** tr<sub>t</sub>.
With a seasonal component choose **m = length of seasonality** (4 quarters, 7 days, 12 months).
Even m → **centred moving average**; odd m = 2p + 1 loses p values at each end.
**Additive** decomposition → **seasonal differences** sd (same units, add up to 0).
**Multiplicative** decomposition → **seasonal indices** si (relative, add up to s).
**Regression approach**: ā = (a1 + a2 + a3)/4, b0 = b0* + ā, sd<sub>j</sub> = a<sub>j</sub> − ā, sd4 = −ā.
must: Moving averages with m = s and seasonal differences / indices
foot: Source: 4ST601 Lecture 6 slides (file slides/text/6-time-series-trends.txt) and Seminar 7 exercises.

questions.q: What does a series of moving averages represent?
questions.e: Moving averages smooth out short-term variation; the smoothed values estimate the trend component.

questions.q: A simple moving average of length m = 7 is used. How many time points at each end have no moving average?
questions.e: m = 2p + 1 = 7 gives p = 3, so the first 3 and the last 3 points are lost.

questions.q: Monthly data with a seasonal pattern. Which length m of moving average should you choose?
questions.e: With a seasonal component, m equals the length of seasonality: 12 months.

questions.q: When do you need a centred moving average?
questions.answer: When m is even (for example 4 or 12)
wrong: When the data have no trend
questions.e: With even m the window has no middle point, so two neighbouring averages are averaged to centre the result on t.

questions.q: Can moving averages be used to predict future values of the time series?
questions.answer: No, the values at the ends of the series are missing
wrong: Yes, but only for quarterly data
questions.e: The lecture lists this as a disadvantage: moving averages cannot predict the future development of a series.

questions.q: In what units are seasonal differences expressed?
questions.answer: In the same units as the time series
questions.e: Seasonal differences come from additive decomposition (y − tr), so they keep the units of the series.

questions.q: A seasonal index for Q1 is 0.693. What does it mean?
questions.answer: Q1 values are on average about 30.7 % below the trend
wrong: Q1 values are 0.693 units below the trend
Q1 values are 69.3 % above the trend
questions.e: Seasonal indices are relative: 0.693 means 69.3 % of the trend value, i.e. about 30.7 % below it.

questions.q: When is additive decomposition (seasonal differences) appropriate?
questions.answer: When seasonal variations are stable in time
wrong: When seasonal variations grow with the level of the series
Only when there is no trend
questions.e: Stable seasonal variations → additive; variations that change in time → multiplicative.

questions.q: What do the seasonal differences of all seasons add up to?
questions.e: Seasonal differences compensate each other over a whole period, so they add up to 0.

questions.q: What do the seasonal indices of all seasons add up to?
questions.e: Seasonal indices are adjusted so that their sum equals s (e.g. 4 for quarters).

questions.q: What is the first step of the simple approach to the seasonal component?
questions.answer: Calculate the trend with moving averages of length m = s
wrong: Run a regression with dummy variables
questions.e: The simple approach first gets tr(t) by moving averages, then works out y − tr or y / tr.

questions.q: How do you get a seasonally adjusted series with seasonal differences?
questions.answer: Subtract the seasonal difference of the season from each value
wrong: Divide each value by the seasonal difference
Add the trend to each value
questions.e: A seasonally adjusted series has the seasonal component removed: y(t) − sd(j).

questions.q: What is special about the regression approach to the seasonal component?
questions.answer: Trend and seasonal component are calculated at the same time
wrong: It does not need any data
questions.e: In the regression approach trend and seasonality are estimated together in one multiple regression with dummy variables.

questions.q: In the regression approach (quarterly data), how is sd4 calculated?
questions.e: The 4th quarter has no dummy (a4 = 0), so sd4 = 0 − ā = −ā.

questions.q: In the regression approach, what is the intercept of the linear trend?
questions.e: The constant from Excel, b0*, must be corrected by the mean of the dummy coefficients: b0 = b0* + ā.

questions.q: Weekly cycle of daily data: 6, 7, 8, 9, 8, 2, 1 (Mon–Sun). What is the first moving average and where does it belong?

vocab.meaning: Mean of a window of m values around time t, moved along the series; the smoothed values estimate the trend.
Moving average of odd length m = 2p + 1: arithmetic mean of p values before t, y(t) and p values after t.
Moving average of even length m = 2p: the mean of two neighbouring windows, so the result belongs to time point t.
The number of values m in each window; with seasonality m equals the length of seasonality s.
The number of seasons in one cycle, s: 4 for quarters, 12 for months, 7 for days of a week.
tr(t): the long-term direction of a time series.
s(t): regular variation within one period (year, week) repeating every season.
y(t) = tr(t) + s(t) + c(t) + e(t); used when seasonal variations are stable in time.
y(t) = tr(t) · s(t) · c(t) · e(t); used when seasonal variations are not stable in time.
sd(j): effect of season j in the units of the series (additive); all seasonal differences add up to 0.
si(j): relative effect of season j (multiplicative), without units; all seasonal indices add up to s.
Seasonal component calculated in separate steps: trend by moving averages, then y − tr or y / tr, then means per season, then adjustment.
Trend and seasonal component calculated together by multiple regression with dummy variables for the seasons.
x(j) = 1 in season j and 0 otherwise; used in the regression approach (the last season has no dummy).
A time series with the seasonal component removed: y(t) − sd(j) or y(t) / si(j).

facts: The smoothed values of a moving average estimate the {trend|seasonal|random|cyclical} component.
A simple moving average of length 7 loses {3|7|1|6} values at each end of the series.
For monthly data with seasonality, the length of the moving average is {12|4|7|3}.
For quarterly data with seasonality, the length of the moving average is {4|12|7|3}.
An even length of the moving average needs a {centred|weighted|simple|exponential} moving average.
Seasonal differences belong to the {additive|multiplicative|linear|quadratic} decomposition.
Seasonal indices belong to the {multiplicative|additive|linear|constant} decomposition.
Seasonal differences of all seasons add up to {0|1|s|100}.
The simple approach first calculates the trend by {moving averages|regression|indices|differences}.
In the regression approach with quarterly data, sd4 equals minus the {mean|sum|maximum|median} of the dummy coefficients.
